implementation_notes: JMS ships the envelope as an API type: every Message carries standard headers (JMSMessageID, JMSCorrelationID, JMSReplyTo, JMSType, ...), an application property set, and a typed body, and the provider enforces the infrastructure requirements the pattern exists for. The Java implementation is therefore mostly 'use the message type the provider gives you': set properties and the correlation id on the outbound message, read them on the inbound side, and hand only the body (getText/getBody) to domain code.
pitfalls: Property names beginning with 'JMS' or 'JMSX' are provider-owned: setting them throws JMSException and they cannot be used for application metadata.
Provider message objects are often pooled and recycled after acknowledge; keeping a reference to the payload past the handler gives you data from another message.
Correlation id and reply-to headers are attacker-controllable on a shared broker - never use them for authorization decisions.

variants.name: Spring Integration Message<T> + MessageHeaders
variants.implementation_notes: When no JMS provider is deployable, Spring's messaging abstraction is the envelope: Message<T> is an immutable payload plus MessageHeaders (a read-only Map with predefined ID/TIMESTAMP/REPLY_CHANNEL/ERROR_CHANNEL keys), built through MessageBuilder and enriched with user headers. Adapters translate to and from the transport, so the same envelope survives several hops; hand-rolled wrapping is unnecessary, but header propagation rules deserve attention because transformations can drop headers.
pitfalls: MessageHeaders is effectively read-only: every mutation throws UnsupportedOperationException, so enrichment means building a new Message.
Header propagation is endpoint-specific: transformers and service activators propagate inbound headers by rule, and a mis-configured handler drops an envelope field without an error.
